title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
summary: Standard dropout neural networks give point predictions and no model uncertainty. The paper proves dropout training is approximate Bayesian inference in a deep Gaussian process, so predictive mean and variance follow from MC dropout—averaging T stochastic forward passes and adding the inverse model precision. Replicating the PBP benchmark on nine UCI regression datasets, MC dropout improves average test RMSE and predictive log-likelihood over Probabilistic Backpropagation and variational Bayes (e.g., Boston Housing RMSE 2.97±0.19 vs PBP 3.01±0.18).

match_target.why: Cheapest faithful target: Boston Housing is the smallest dataset (N=506) with a 50-unit single-hidden-layer net and ~400 epochs, yet it is the paper's headline regression result (MC-dropout RMSE 2.97±0.19 beats PBP 3.01±0.18 and VI 4.32±0.29) and matches the user's hint exactly.

tolerance.why: Rule 1: Table 1 reports a standard error of 0.19 over the 20 splits for Boston Housing dropout RMSE; 3 x 0.19 = 0.57, kept at the 2-decimal precision the paper prints.

requirements.stmt: Estimate the predictive distribution by MC dropout: sample T sets of Bernoulli dropout masks and average the stochastic forward passes for the mean.
requirements.quote: In practice this is equivalent to performing T stochastic forward passes through the network and averaging the results.

requirements.stmt: The Table 1 RMSE must be computed from MC-dropout averaged predictions (eq. 6), not from standard dropout weight averaging.
requirements.quote: Dropout's RMSE in table 1 is given by averaging stochastic forward passes through the network following eq. (6) (MC dropout).

requirements.stmt: Predictive variance equals the sample variance of the T stochastic forward passes plus the inverse model precision tau^-1.
requirements.quote: which equals the sample variance of T stochastic forward passes through the NN plus the inverse model precision.

requirements.stmt: Predictive log-likelihood is estimated by Monte Carlo integration using a log-sum-exp over the T stochastic forward passes (eq. 8).
requirements.quote: We can estimate our predictive log-likelihood by Monte Carlo integration of eq. (2).

requirements.stmt: Model precision tau is tied to weight decay lambda and prior length-scale l by the identity tau = sqrt(l^2/(2N*lambda)) (eq. 7).
Set the prior length-scale l to 1e-2 for most datasets.
requirements.quote: set the prior length-scale to 10−2 for most datasets based on the range of the data

requirements.stmt: Find the optimal model precision tau by Bayesian optimisation over validation log-likelihood, using 40 BO iterations.
requirements.quote: we use Bayesian optimisation (BO, (Snoek et al., 2012; Snoek & authors, 2015)) over validation log-likelihood to find optimal τ

requirements.stmt: Use a single hidden layer with 50 units, following the PBP setup.
Apply dropout before every weight layer with the stated small probabilities (0.05 and 0.005).
requirements.quote: We used dropout with probabilities 0.05 and 0.005 since the network size is very small

requirements.stmt: Train with mini-batches of size 32 using the Adam optimiser.
requirements.quote: Finally, we used mini-batches of size 32 and the Adam optimiser (Kingma & Ba, 2014).

requirements.stmt: Run 40 BO iterations, then train the final model with 10x more iterations (400 epochs) at the selected tau.
requirements.quote: The BO runs used 40 iterations following the original setup, but after finding the optimal parameter values we used 10x more iterations

requirements.stmt: Average results over 20 random splits of the data (5 for Protein Structure, 1 for Year Prediction MSD).
requirements.quote: All experiments were averaged on 20 random splits of the data

requirements.stmt: Replicate the experimental setup of Hernandez-Lobato & Adams (2015) for the regression benchmarks.
requirements.quote: We replicate the experiment set-up in Hernández-Lobato & Adams (2015) and compare the RMSE and predictive log-likelihood of dropout

requirements.stmt: Use the standard dropout objective (NN loss plus L2 weight decay); with the precision/length-scale setting it recovers the GP-MC objective of eq. (1).
requirements.quote: Setting E(yn, by(xn, bωn)) = −log p(yn|xn, bωn)/τ we recover eq. (1) for an appropriate setting of the precision hyper-parameter τ and length-scale l.

requirements.stmt: Do not adapt the model structure; use dropout exactly as in current practice and only evaluate uncertainty at test time.
requirements.quote: We used dropout following the same way the method would be used in current research – without adapting model structure.
